title: Janus looks both ways
hookLine: the Romans named January for Janus, who looks backward and forward

cards: Stand in a doorway for a moment. Behind you, the room you're leaving. In front, the room you're walking into.

For a second you're in neither, and you can see both. Ancient Romans gave that spot its own god. His name was Janus, and on coins and statues he has two faces, one looking back and one looking forward.
The doorway, the gate and the first day of the year all belonged to him. Our word January still carries his name.

teach.h: JANUS: GOD OF DOORS AND BEGINNINGS.
teach.b: First, who he was to the Romans.
Janus was the god of beginnings and passages: doors, gates, the start of things. In Roman worship his name was often called first in prayers, before other gods, because he stood at the opening.
The poet Ovid, in his poem on the Roman calendar, has Janus explain his two faces like a doorkeeper who watches both the street and the house. Second, a well-known door.
In Rome, the gates of a small shrine to Janus stood open in wartime and closed in peace. They were rarely closed; the emperor Augustus boasted that they'd been shut three times in his rule.
Third, what a Stoic would make of two faces. Seneca observes that fear and hope march together, and both come from a mind that leans ahead instead of standing in the present.
Marcus reminds himself that the only life anyone loses is the moment they're living now.
So a Stoic might say: look both ways, yes, but don't move into either room. Fourth, looking well.

teach.h: BACK TO LEARN, AHEAD TO PREPARE.
teach.b: Look back to learn, not to replay: what went right, what would you do differently?

Look forward to prepare, not to worry: what's one thing to do next? Then step through into the room that's real, which is this one. Janus himself stands in the threshold, after all, not in the past or the future.

how: Some people mark a new year or a transition by deliberately looking back at what they learned and forward to one clear step, then returning attention to the present.

o: a two-faced trickster who could never be trusted
a Roman god of war who guarded the city's walls
the Roman god of doorways, facing back and forward

p: a poem on the Roman calendar

s: January takes its name from Janus
the god of beginnings and doorways.
the gates of Janus's shrine in Rome were usually closed
they were open in wartime, and Rome was rarely at peace; Augustus boasted they were shut three times in his rule.
Seneca and Marcus told readers to live mostly in the future
both warned about leaning into the past or the future instead of the present.

games.q: you're at the threshold of a new year. how would a Stoic use Janus's two faces?
o: replay every mistake of the past year
look back to learn, forward to prepare, then live today
plan every detail of the coming year
games.why: the past and future are for learning and preparing; the life you actually have is the present moment.

practice: Stand in a real doorway if you can, or picture one. Look back over the last few months for one thing you learned, then turn and look forward for one small, clear thing you want to do.
Then come back to the doorway itself and feel your feet on the threshold, the only place you ever actually stand.

wordCard.voice: Janus, the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, with one face to the past and one to the future, who gave January its name. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: January, the month of Janus.

carryVoice: Your line: both ways. A glance back, a glance ahead, and then the room you're in. Day six hundred sixty-six.
